title: OpenAI compatibility: tool handoff sanitization and latency-aware choice heuristics
author: Aisha Raman
description:
Motivation: We observed intermittent failures and latency spikes when LLMs returned tool invocation payloads that contained nested or unexpected metadata (PII, verbose stack traces, or binary blobs) combined with fragmented streaming deltas. This causes downstream tool adapters (3rd-party webhooks and internal connectors) to error or timeout and complicates OpenAI-compat streaming where clients expect deterministic 'tool' messages.

Summary: This PR introduces a lightweight handoff sanitization pipeline and a latency-aware tool selection heuristic in the OpenAI compatibility layer. The sanitizer normalizes the tool invocation envelope, strips/flags unsafe fields (configurable allowlist), and coalesces fragmented streaming frames into a canonical final handoff message. The latency heuristic prefers low-latency local adapters when request SLOs are tight and gracefully falls back to higher-capacity remote tools when throughput/quality tradeoffs are favorable.

Changes included: 1) openai_compat/compat_handoff_adapter.go: new adapter glue that normalizes incoming function/tool outputs into a canonical "tool_handoff" envelope; it attaches provenance metadata and a sanitization report for auditing. 2) openai_compat/stream_reassembly.go: streaming frame coalescer that buffers fragmented tool frames up to a configurable window and emits a merged delta used by the adapter. 3) runtime/tool_handoff/sanitizer.go: configurable sanitizer with allowlist/denylist rules, PII scrubbing hooks (KMS-based redaction is pluggable), and size guards to reject oversized payloads early. 4) benchmarks/latency/hand_off_bench.py: microbenchmarks showing median improvement in failed-tool call rate (-67%) and 95th percentile end-to-end tool latency (-22%) for small streaming fragments. 5) tests/integration/tool_handoff_test.go + unit tests for sanitization and heuristic fallbacks. 6) docs/api/openai-tool-handoff.md: new docs page describing compatibility guarantees and migration notes. 7) rollout flag in console/rollouts/feature_flags.yaml to gate the heuristic.

Compatibility and safety: The sanitizer is opt-in via feature flag and defaults to a permissive allowlist that only removes obviously unsafe binary/prototype fields. We added a monitoring counter (hand_off.sanitizer.actions) and an alert runbook when >1% of calls are sanitized for a given tenant. PII redaction is opt-in and requires a KMS key configured on Private/Dedicated deployments.

Testing and CI: Extensive unit and integration tests added. CI run summary: build (pass), unit-tests (pass), go-lint (pass), integration (pass). Benchmarks run locally and included as artifacts.

Rollout plan: 1) Enable feature flag for internal canary (redwood-internal) for 48 hours. 2) Monitor sanitizer rate, downstream adapter errors, and 95/99 latency histograms. 3) Gradually enable for 10%, 50%, then 100% of hosted traffic with a rollback playbook if error rate increases.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation and unit tests - [x] Integration tests with streaming fragments - [x] Benchmarks and perf numbers - [x] Feature-flag gating and rollout docs - [x] Release notes entry

Notes: This PR does not change the external API contract for successful tool invocations; it only mutates the intermediate handoff envelope when the sanitizer rules match (and records the mutation in the audit metadata). The latency-aware chooser sits in the routing layer and only influences which compatible tool endpoint is selected; it will not re-route mid-invocation. For Private deployments without KMS configured, PII redaction is disabled and sanitizer falls back to size-based guarding.
commits: Initial sanitizer implementation and adapter glue
Add streaming frame coalescer and buffer window
Add allowlist/denylist config and PII redaction hooks
Unit and integration tests for various edge cases
Add benchmarks and docs; wire feature flag for rollout
review_comments: Marta Kline: Please clarify how this interacts with existing KV cache / prefix caching. If we coalesce frames we need to make sure cache keys remain stable.

Aisha Raman (author): Reply - sanitizer does not modify semantic prompt prefixes used by the KV cache; it only touches the tool_handoff envelope outside of the cached token prefixes. Added explicit tests to assert cache key invariants.
Ethan Cho: Can the allowlist be tenant-scoped? We should avoid a one-size-fits-all for enterprise customers with strict compliance needs.
Aisha Raman (author): Reply - yes; allowlist/denylist are injectable per-tenant via console flags in Dedicated/Private and default to org-global for hosted. Documented in the migration notes.
Priya Anand: Observability looks good; consider a histogram for sanitizer processing time to ensure it doesn't add tail latency.
Aisha Raman (author): Reply - added hand_off.sanitizer.latency histogram and included it in the canary dashboards.
Marta Kline: Approved after the cache-key tests and latency histogram were added.
release_notes: Added OpenAI-compat handoff sanitizer and latency-aware tool routing. Opt-in feature flag, improved robustness for fragmented streaming tool messages, and tenant-scoped sanitization controls. See docs/api/openai-tool-handoff.md for migration steps.
